extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing fiction writers (novelists and short-story writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, revision-focused guidance for writing and editing fiction prose (short stories and novels), emphasizing language, technique, and the writer’s daily practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime Rule: write a lot and read a lot
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a lot and read a lot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King repeatedly states this as the fundamental rule (the “Prime Rule”). He supplies an extended booklist of works he’s read recently that influenced him, and frames wide reading as essential input for improving one’s writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit needless words
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King explicitly endorses The Elements of Style and uses Strunk’s injunction as a touchstone for revision: many changes are cuts intended to speed the story. He notes most edits are cuts and tries to follow Strunk in pruning excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: The editor is always right (but use judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The editor is always right.” Corollary: no writer will take all of his or her editor’s advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King urges deference to editorial judgment—'to write is human, to edit is divine'—while acknowledging writers will not accept every change. He models trusting an experienced editor (credits Chuck Verrill) while also implying the writer keeps final artistic decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Draft = First Draft - 10%
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King gives this concrete revision target and demonstrates it with a before/after example. Many of his edits are aggressive cuts aimed at tightening, removing excess, and improving pace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce important elements early (Chekhov’s gun)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce props/objects/keys early if they play a part later. (‘If there’s a gun on the mantel in Act I, it must go off in Act III.’)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He gives the example of moving the protagonist’s lucky Hawaiian shirt earlier in the story so it doesn’t feel like a deus ex machina when it’s used later. The principle: plant important details early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t do the reader’s thinking for them
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King points out passages where he was 'doing a lot of the reader’s thinking for him' and cuts those lines. Trust the reader's intelligence; remove needless explanatory scaffolding that slows the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut stage directions, belaboring, and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove excessive stage direction, belaboring of the obvious, and needless repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In his revision notes he explicitly cuts ‘too much stage direction, too much belaboring of the obvious, and too much clumsy back story.’ The aim is to speed narrative flow and remove redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary adverbs (allow exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stomp unnecessary adverbs; permit rare exceptions where they serve characterization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King demonstrates cutting adverbs (he 'stomped' an adverb like 'shortly') but retains an adverb ('heartily') in one spot because it clarifies tone/character. Rule: generally avoid -ly modifiers, but keep them when they carry real work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prune clumsy backstory; integrate it organically
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid clumsy or heavy-handed backstory inserts; add background only where it clarifies and belongs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He cut clumsy back story from the first draft and instead added only what clarified character. Backstory should be economical and serve present action or characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose names and details with medium/audience in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Select names/details with practical considerations (readability, ear for audio, length) in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King changed the long name 'Ostermeyer' to the shorter 'Olin' for economy and because he anticipated reading the stories aloud. Consider how names and details will perform in other contexts (audio, stage, memory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise; shorter can mean less bullshit
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor brevity; shorter, cleaner prose reduces bullshit and clarifies craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King criticizes many long how-to books on writing and praises short direct guides (e.g., Elements of Style). He argues the shorter the book, the less bullshit, and uses brevity as a virtue in both advice and fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use revision to ‘dress’ the story: raw first draft, lean second draft
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the first draft as raw material; revision is where the story gets dressed, tightened, and clarified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King presents a raw 'door shut' first draft and a revised 'door open' second draft, walking through specific edits and why they were made. The process model: write freely, then revise ruthlessly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do research but avoid trite or irrelevant details
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the necessary research to lend authenticity, but remove trite or irrelevant details that add nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He notes research (e.g., the Dolphin opened in October 1910) and also cuts trite flourishes (e.g., 'Have a cigar! They’re Cuban!' as movie‑style cliché). Use research to ground the story; omit clichés that distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title and naming are important but can change
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles and names may be placeholders; a better title often occurs later or is supplied by an editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King placed a working title into his draft knowing a better one might occur or an editor might change it. Don’t fixate prematurely on perfect titles; they can be refined later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing’s purpose: enrich readers’ lives (not fame or money)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing isn’t about making money, getting famous, or social rewards; it’s about enriching readers’ lives and your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King frames the writer’s motive as service to readers and personal enrichment. This is a normative criterion for why and how one should approach the craft—aim for work that matters to readers, not merely self-promotion.
